New paper from Salesforce AI Research and Datadog on how research agents use GPUs. This matters a lot if your agents run experiments on GPUs. (bookmark it) They built ComputeWise, a benchmark with a simulated GPU that replays recorded training runs, so hundreds of agent experiments can run without real hardware. Unaided, agents spent only 52% of GPU time on the work needed for the final answer. 22% went to unneeded runs, and 26% sat idle. Keeping GPUs busy did not fix it. Of 24 runs with GPUs at least 90% busy, 16 still took 25% or more longer than a comparison schedule. Hints and a job scheduler did not remove the waste either. A harness did. The model states what evidence it needs and judges the results, while plain code dispatches the jobs. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31027 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/computewise-measuring-and-fixing-gpu-waste-by-ai-research-agents-2611.31027

Great paper from HKUST and NVIDIA on harness design for autoresearch agents. (bookmark it) If you build research agents that run experiments over many attempts, this is a good read. Very practical. Their MLEvolver harness reaches a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and 94% on KernelBench Level 3, ahead of AIDE and OpenEvolve at the same inference budget. They tested each memory mechanism separately against a simple recency-truncation baseline, with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol. For context, keeping a separate record of each past attempt beat a rolling summary. Context folding, which condenses each attempt into a short digest, was best in all six settings, up to 19.2% over the baseline. For skills, deleting lessons the agent didn't use gave the largest average gain, ahead of merging them or turning them into standing rules. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28244 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/demystifying-the-autoresearch-harness-how-context-and-skills-shape-self-evolving-2611.28244

Great practical paper from the University of Waterloo on agent costs. To lower agent costs, you want the frontier model to lead every task, with a small local model handling routine subtasks. (bookmark it) Delegent is built on Claude Code. The frontier model plans and makes the main coding changes. It hands code reading, test runs, and corpus search to subagents running a small language model on your own hardware. With a 27B FP8 model, frontier cost fell 67% on long-horizon coding and 59% on agentic search, with no loss in task performance. A 2B model that fits on a laptop still cut coding cost by 66%. No router or model was trained. One short instruction, which keeps the main coding tasks with the frontier model, accounts for most of the savings. At API prices, the 27B model adds 3 to 10 cents per coding task. If your agent bill is high, check how much of the frontier model's spend goes to reading files and running tests, and move that work to a local model. Banger paper from NVIDIA on sandboxes for agent exploration. (bookmark it) Sandboxes are an important primitive for scaling with agents. There are some interesting ideas here for supporting stateful agent exploration. It live-forks an entire running container, including processes, memory, files, and network, using copy-on-write. Clones share the pages that stay the same, and only the pages that change use new memory. It needs no root access, kernel changes, or hardware virtualization, and runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows through WSL 2. TimeTravelContainer cloned EDA tool environments 84.1x faster, cut memory by 31 to 72%, and sped up end-to-end agent runs by 1.7 to 9.4x. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32255 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/timetravelcontainer-a-live-forking-sandbox-for-stateful-agent-exploration-2611.32255
